newsitem.title: USA: Miami woes not affecting tourist services - mayor.
newsitem.headline: Miami woes not affecting tourist services - mayor.

text.p: The mayor of Florida's Dade County sought to reassure potential visitors on Thursday that Miami's financial mess has not affected the larger metropolitan area and its tourism-dependent economy.

"I'm very concerned with the national and international headlines. For the national and international community, there is no difference between Miami and Miami Beach and Dade County," Mayor Alex Penelas said. "The city of Miami is our flagship city and we all suffer from the consequences."

Miami is the Dade County seat but is only one of 29 independent municipalities in the sprawling conurbation generally covered by the Miami label. The city has a $68 million deficit for the year that began Oct. 1 and suffered the ignominy Tuesday of having the governor put it under guardianship of state advisers.

Penelas called a news conference to announce the county would help the city by continuing to offer a $10 million loan first suggested in October and by offering to buy some prime city-owned waterfront land targeted for a basketball arena.

The mayor said the county, which has already loaned a dozen budget executives to the city, was prepared to provide police and other services if the city was forced to cut back. He also said he would appoint a commission of government, business and community leaders to draft a contingency plan to provide all public services to Miami if the city is dissolved "either by vote or through complete financial collapse."

"I am not in favour of abolishing our signature city of Miami," Penelas said. "We stand committed to help the city of Miami through its problems. This financial crisis is serious but it is also manageable."

But he expressed concern that Miami's fiscal disgrace would deter visitors, crippling the county's $8.5 billion tourism industry. Miami accounted for only two percent of the county's area and 17 percent of its population.

Miami International Airport, the Port of Miami, the public hospital and the tourist police programme are run by the county and are all unaffected by Miami's budget crunch, he said. "Dade County's fiscal position continues to be strong and healthy."
Tourism and business officials said Miami's woes had not hurt the area's economy so far.
"Businesses are continuing to look at Miami as a viable location for their headquarters," Carol Wyllie, head of the Beacon Council economic development group, said.
Robert Beatty of the Greater Miami Visitors and Convention Bureau said, "1996 was a banner year for the tourism industry. Even with these problems we expect 1997 to be even better."

Nor has Dade County's credit rating been affected. While Miami's rating was cut to non-investment grade or "junk" status, the county's general obligation debt is rated A-1 by Moody's Investor Service and A-plus by Standard & Poor's Corp.
The ratings signify "strong capacity to pay interest and repay principle," and "upper-medium grade obligations."

The county, set to price a $120 million solid waste bond issue next week, has received assurances from financial advisers that "The rating agencies and the investors are aware of the difference" between Dade County and Miami, assistant county manager David Morris said. "We think we'll get the same good prices as we always do," he said.
